newsitem.title: USA: U.S. July production seen moderate, risk to upside.
newsitem.headline: U.S. July production seen moderate, risk to upside.

text.p: U.S. industrial production was expected to have grown at a steady pace in July despite evidence of a softer manufacturing sector in the month's employment report, economists said.
But they warned that the data, to be released Thursday, might well be stronger than expected following a recent jump in the National Association of Purchasing Management index.
A small rise as expected would confirm a sustainable, moderate rate of economic growth and do little to sway Federal Reserve interest rate policy in either direction.

Economists in a Reuters survey, on average, said industrial production rose 0.2 percent in July on the heels of a 0.3 percent rise in June. Capacity utilization, meanwhile, was seen holding steady at a 83.5 percent rate.
The data was to be released by the Federal Reserve at 0915 EDT/1315 GMT on Thursday.

John Ryding, senior economist at Bear Stearns & Co, noted that a relatively soft read of manufacturing hours in the latest employment report may reflect summer shut-downs and not necessarily be a good indication of July production.
In the employment report, manufacturing payrolls fell 5,000 in July, while average weekly manufacturing hours worked per week fell to 41.7 from 41.8.
Ryding and other economists said the risk was to the upside following the jump in the National Association of Purchasing Management index to a 2-1/2 year high of 58.6 in July from 55.7 in June.
More recently, the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta's index of industry business activity on Tuesday also suggested some strength, surging to 23.3 in July from 15.3 in June.

"The (NAPM and Atlanta Fed) surveys show a livlier sector than some of the other data do, so it wouldn't surprise me to see a higher number," said Carol Stone, director and deputy chief economist at Nomura Securities. She noted that hard information from the employment report did not show that "ebullience."

Production data in line with her forecast for a 0.3 percent rise, Stone said, would present a favorable picture of U.S. economic health. Such a rise would not be enough to prompt a pickup in capacity use, she said, and would certainly be far from a level seen as fueling higher inflation.
"That's a good growth trend and it's right along the trend in capacity growth so that capacity utilization should remain steady," Stone said.
Utility output may skew the number higher given the relatively warm month of July, some economists said.
Inventories, which had been pumped up in the second quarter, may exert some softening pressure on production in July and months ahead, Stone said.
"The magnitude of inventory building was well above what is widely accepted as being necessary to maintain the regular pace of business," she said.

Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest, said "no shortage" of inventories may lead to a slower rate of inventory production. On the other hand, Sohn said a recent pickup in retail sales and evidence of better auto sales could mean an acceleration in inventory building.

"When sales are good, manufacturers have to produce faster not only to meet existing sales but also to build inventories slightly, so I wouldn't be surprised to see a slight acceleration in the third quarter," Sohn said.
